content:
Doom spending is buying things you know you shouldn't, not because you lack discipline, but because the future looks bleak enough that saving feels pointless. India's Gen Z is stuck in this loop right now, and UPI's frictionless payments have made it easier than ever to act on the impulse before doubt can catch up.

Key Takeaways

  • Doom spending is emotionally driven buying rooted in financial futility, not poor willpower
  • 87% of young Indians report growing financial uncertainty, creating ideal conditions for this pattern
  • UPI's frictionless design lowers the barrier on impulse buys to nearly zero
  • The anxiety-to-purchase cycle feels rational in the moment but compounds financial stress over time
  • A 48-hour wait rule and a fixed guilt-free monthly budget are the two most practical interruptions

What Is Doom Spending, Exactly?

Doom spending is buying things to cope with financial futility. It's different from impulse buying because the logic is deliberate: if homeownership feels permanently out of reach, spending 800 rupees on something enjoyable today feels rational. Financial therapists reported a 43% increase in doom spending cases in 2026.

It's not the same as bad money habits. The doom spender often understands their financial situation clearly. That clarity is partly the problem.

The pattern plays out like this: a layoff headline or a property price check triggers a feeling of financial helplessness. The easiest exit from that feeling is a purchase. It works for about 20 minutes. Then guilt arrives, which feeds back into the original anxiety. Then another purchase.

Why Can't India's Young Adults Stop Doom Spending?

Three specific pressures have converged in 2026. Home ownership feels mathematically impossible. Job security in IT and services is genuinely uncertain after two years of layoffs. And with 87% of Indians reporting growing financial uncertainty, the sense that the future is not worth saving for is widespread, even if not fully conscious.

Housing is the sharpest pressure point. A decent 2BHK in Bengaluru costs 80 to 100 lakh. Someone earning 8 lakh a year, saving aggressively, needs close to a decade just for a down payment. That math doesn't resolve into hope. It produces a kind of resignation: if the goal is unreachable, why delay smaller pleasures for it?

Job anxiety makes it worse. India's IT sector went through significant layoff waves in 2025 and into 2026. When you're not confident your income will exist in 18 months, long-term saving loses its emotional grip. Short-term comfort starts winning that argument.

And then there's UPI. Handing over physical cash creates a moment of hesitation. Tapping UPI creates none. That invisibility lets doom spending happen accross many small transactions before the week even registers as heavy.

Doom Spending vs. Mindful Spending

FactorDoom SpendingMindful Spending
Main triggerAnxiety, helplessness, bad newsDeliberate choice or genuine need
Decision speedSeconds, mostly unplannedConsidered, often delayed
Feeling afterBrief relief, then guiltNeutral or satisfied
Long-term effectCompounds financial stressAligns with financial goals
Typical platformUPI, quick commerce appsPlanned purchases, intentional EMI

The Loop That Keeps It Going

Anxiety hits. A purchase provides short relief. Your brain registers the purchase as the solution and stores that pattern. Next time anxiety hits, the same solution gets tried. It's neccessary to name this directly because most financial advice skips it and jumps to "make a budget," which doesn't address why the budget keeps breaking.

The loop is hard to interrupt mid-cycle. The impulse feels rational in the moment. And partly, it is. Spending on something enjoyable beats sitting with acute financial anxiety for an hour. The problem is the cycle doesn't end with the purchase. It restarts.

Interrupting it means adding friction before the tap, not regret after:

  • A 48-hour rule for any unplanned purchase above 500 rupees. Still want it in two days? Consider it then.
  • A fixed monthly guilt-free amount, say 2,000 to 3,000 rupees, that you can spend freely without tracking.
  • Turning off UPI notifications from quick commerce apps. Removing the trigger works better than resisting it.
  • Moving shopping apps off your home screen. Out of sight genuinely helps at 11 pm when willpower is lowest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is doom spending the same as retail therapy?

Not exactly. Retail therapy is buying to lift your mood. Doom spending is buying because saving for the future feels irrational. The emotional flavor is different: retail therapy is about pleasure, doom spending is about futility. Both can compound financial stress, but doom spending typically runs deeper and is harder to spot as a pattern.

Does doom spending affect your CIBIL score?

It can, indirectly. High credit card utilization from heavy spending months, and EMI defaults after a doom spending streak, both lower your CIBIL score. The damage builds gradually as spending regularly outpaces income and your financial cushion narrows month by month.

What triggers doom spending most often in India?

Property price news, social media posts showing peers buying homes or traveling, sale notifications from quick commerce platforms, and late-night scrolling. UPI's always-on access makes late-night the riskiest window. Tiredness lowers inhibition, and frictionless payment removes what little resistance remains.

How is doom spending different from just being bad with money?

Being bad with money usually means poor planning or low financial literacy. Doom spending happens even when someone understands their finances clearly. The driver is anxiety about a bleak-feeling future, not ignorance of the present. This matters because the fix is behavioral, not just a better spreadsheet.

Can a fixed doom spending budget actually help?

Yes, and often more than trying to eliminate impulse spending entirely. Giving yourself a defined monthly amount you can spend freely removes the guilt cycle. When impulse spending has a container, the post-purchase guilt doesn't feed back into the anxiety loop the same way. Start small: 2,000 to 3,000 rupees a month.

The Short Version

Doom spending isn't recklessness. It's what happens when saving for the future stops feeling worth it. For a lot of young Indians in 2026, that feeling is completely understandable: housing is expensive, job security is uncertain, and UPI makes it frictionless to act on anxiety. Recognizing the loop is the first step. Adding friction before the next tap is the second. The goal isn't to stop spending on small pleasures. It's to spend when you chose to, not when your anxiety decided for you.
